Chapter 5: Learning from History and Other Cultures.
Have you ever noticed how, in today’s world, we tend to keep death at arm’s length? For so many of us, it’s something we avoid talking about—almost like if we don’t see it, maybe it won’t touch us.
But that wasn’t always the case. In earlier times, and in other places around the world, death was out in the open—woven right into the daily rhythm of life. Families cared for their loved ones at home, held heartfelt rituals, and discovered meaning through mourning together.
Working in the funeral industry really brings these differences into focus. The staff meets families from all kinds of backgrounds, each bringing their own unique traditions and beliefs. Some families want the classic service—embalming, a polished casket, maybe a line of cars heading to the cemetery. Others choose something simpler, like a quiet cremation with no ceremony at all. And then there are those who draw from their own cultures—maybe ritual washings, special prayers, or personal offerings.
Imagine this: one afternoon, a family arrives with a set of rituals the staff has never seen before. There’s a little pause—a moment where everyone wonders how to honor these wishes while still following the funeral home’s rules. So, what happens? The staff listens. They ask questions. And together, they find a way to make space for what matters most to the family. It’s a powerful reminder that there’s no single “right” way to grieve. There’s no universal script for saying goodbye.
The history of death rituals is incredibly rich and varied. In some places, people honor the dead with joyful celebrations—feasts, laughter, songs that echo through the night. In others, mourning is deeply solemn, marked by quiet reflection and gentle silence. What the staff learns, over and over, is that these rituals have a purpose. They give the living something to hold onto—a way to find comfort, and maybe a little sense, in the face of loss.
Compare that to many modern funerals, which can feel, well, a bit sterile. The focus is often on efficiency, on keeping everything hidden away. But here’s the thing—when the process is too removed, families can end up feeling lost and disconnected, unsure of how to grieve or where to put their pain. The staff sees it in the eyes of those who leave the funeral home still searching for meaning, still waiting for closure that never quite comes.
Over time, it becomes clear: there’s real value in looking to the past, in learning from how other cultures have faced death. The staff starts weaving pieces of these traditions into their own work—inviting families to take part, to find their own way of saying goodbye. Sure, there are guidelines and expectations to balance. It’s not always a smooth path. But when families are given the chance to grieve in their own way, something changes. The experience becomes richer, more personal—more real.
So, what’s the takeaway here? Death touches everyone, but the ways we respond are as unique as each life. By opening ourselves up—by learning from history and from the world around us—we can create a more honest, compassionate approach to saying goodbye.
The journey isn’t over. But every step brings deeper understanding, a greater sense of connection, and a chance to fully embrace what it means to be human.
